title: The discovery of electricity
subtitle: From Franklin to Tesla
subject: sciences
description: Electricity was not invented in one stroke. It was first observed, then understood, then tamed. Here are the key steps.

hero.hook: From lightning to the smartphone: two centuries to tame the invisible.

blocks.text: Electricity exists in nature: lightning, electric fish, the crackle of friction. What changed the world was learning to **produce** it, to **transport** it, and to put it to work.
That story runs across more than two centuries, full of risky experiments and bitter rivalries.

In the 18th century, **Benjamin Franklin** showed that lightning is an electrical phenomenon. His kite experiment, often told in a romanticized version, was meant to prove that the sky and the laboratory friction machine were playing with the same force.

blocks.caption: Franklin ties lightning to electricity: a dangerous idea, and a founding one

blocks.text: The same years produced the **lightning rod**, a metal spike that offers lightning a safe path to the ground. Electricity left the realm of mystery and entered engineering.

sections.title: Faraday and the making of current

blocks.text: In the 19th century, **Michael Faraday** showed that a magnet moving near a wire can create an electric current. This is **induction**. Without that idea there is no dynamo, no alternator, no modern power plant.

blocks.caption: Faraday turns motion and magnetism into current

blocks.text: Faraday came from a modest family and started out as a bookbinder. He learned his science by reading the books he bound.

At the end of the 19th century, two camps faced off. **Thomas Edison** pushed direct current. **Nikola Tesla** and the Westinghouse company backed alternating current, which is easier to carry over long distances.

blocks.caption: Alternating current wins the job of powering cities

blocks.text: Alternating current won the urban networks. Cities lit up. Factories changed their rhythm.
Today electricity runs hospitals, trains, the Internet, refrigerators. The challenge is no longer only to produce it, but to produce it cleanly and reliably.
Electricity was first understood, then tamed: Franklin for lightning, Faraday for generating current, Tesla and alternating current for bringing it into homes. Our daily life still depends on it.
